Victorian Literature. The literary output of England during Queen Victoria's reign from 1837 to 1901, a period of unprecedented economic expansion, imperial power, scientific progress, and deep social anxiety that produced some of the most influential works in Western literature.

This was the age of the novel's formal perfection. Charles Dickens, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, the Bronte sisters: these writers combined realism with emotional depth and formal innovation. They explored contemporary social problems while also creating characters of unprecedented psychological complexity. They invented the modern novel's capacity to represent the internal lives of people in all their contradiction.

The novel became capable of doing things it had never done before. It could follow a character's thoughts minute by minute. It could represent desire and anxiety and moral confusion. It could embed social critique within intimate family drama. And simultaneously it was entertainment, sold to mass audiences, serialized in periodicals, read aloud in parlors.

Detective fiction originated as a Victorian form. Edgar Allan Poe pioneered it in America, but it crystallized in Victorian England through Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes. The detective story became one of literature's most enduring forms, still followed by writers today. Holmes embodied Victorian faith in reason while the stories revealed reason's limitations.

Gothic literature experienced a major revival during this period. Writers blended earlier Gothic terror with contemporary anxieties about science, sexuality, and degeneration. Frankenstein found new life. Dracula, published in 1897 by Bram Stoker, brought Gothic nightmares into modern times. Science could create life or animate the dead. Ancient evils could reach into the present.

The Victorian period witnessed intense debates about women's roles and sexuality and morality. These debates shaped the literature. Complex female characters appeared in novels, questioning their prescribed roles. The New Woman emerged as both literary figure and social threat: educated, independent, resistant to traditional submission.

Victorian poetry maintained rigorous formal structures—sonnets, dramatic monologues—while tackling modern themes: doubt about religion, alienation from industrial society, anxiety about empire's moral cost. The form was traditional but the content was radically questioning.

By the 1880s and 1890s, rebellion emerged from within Victorian literature itself. Aestheticism and Decadence rejected Victorian earnestness. Early Modernism questioned Victorian certainty. Writers began to doubt that the novel could represent reality at all. This crisis of confidence in Victorian conventions created the conditions for Modernism. Victorian literature had achieved such perfection that the only way forward was rupture.
